blocks.text: …take her out of the state as her guardian?"
I watched the security footage again. The baseball cap. The way she tucked her hair behind one ear. Then I knew why her face looked familiar.

We hadn't spoken in four years. Dana has bipolar disorder. When she's well, she's funny, generous, the best aunt in the world. When she stops her medication, she becomes convinced of things that aren't true. The last time, she believed my husband was dangerous to my daughter and called child services on us. The report was dismissed. I asked her to stay away until she got treatment.

She'd picked up my wallet at the mall, the day I lost it. She'd followed me there. In her mind, she was planning a rescue. She believed my daughter was in danger and that she had to take her somewhere "safe" in another state.

She'd rented the first minivan to practice the route. The blood on the seats was hers. She'd cut her hand badly on a broken car seat she was trying to install. The pink hair clip was one my daughter had left in Dana's car years ago. She'd kept it.
The second rental was for the next morning, a few hours after my daughter's school opened.

Police found Dana at a motel near the airport that evening. She didn't resist. She sat on the bed and cried and said, "I just wanted her to be safe." Officers took her to a hospital for a psychiatric evaluation instead of jail.
She was hospitalized for three weeks. A judge ordered her into treatment and issued a protective order for my daughter. The identity theft charges were reduced when she completed the program.
Dana wrote me a letter six months later.

She's back on medication and living in a supportive housing program. She said she was horrified by what she'd almost done. I believe her. We talk on the phone now, carefully. She hasn't seen my daughter yet. Maybe someday, with a counselor in the room.
My daughter knows only that Aunt Dana was very sick and is getting better. She drew her a card with a sun on it. I mailed it.
If someone you love is in a mental health crisis, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
